newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua has devastating history of misery.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua has devastating history of misery.

text.p: Nicaragua, where voters on Sunday will elect a new president, has a devastating history of poverty, corruption and brutality. Following are key facts about the country and a summary of its recent history.
Area: 48,800 square miles (130,245 square km)
Geography: Nicaragua is bounded by Honduras to the north, Costa Rica to the south, the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Caribbean Sea to the east.
Population: 4.14 million (1995 census).
Capital city: Managua.
Language: Spanish is the official language. Some people on the Caribbean coast speak Creole English and Miskito Indians also have their own language.
Religion: Predominantly Roman Catholic.
Number of voters: 2.4 million
Economy: GDP: US$2 billion.
GDP per capita: US$470 (World Bank figure).
Economic growth: 4 percent (1995). The government sees
4.6 percent for 1996.
Inflation: 11.5 percent (1995). 11 percent seen for 1996.
Currency: The cordoba. Current exchange rate: 8.72
cordobas = one U.S. dollar.
Foreign debt: $10.3 billion (World Bank figure).
Armed forces: About 15,000 soldiers. Before 1990, the armed forces had 100,000 members.

Election facts: Voters will choose a new president, vice president, National Assembly, mayors and town councils. If no presidential candidate gets 45 percent of the vote, a runoff election between the two top vote-getters will be held.
The Oct. 20 election is the first time a civilian, freely elected government will hand over power to another such government in undisputed circumstances.
NICARAGUA'S HISTORY:
1838 -- Nicaragua gains independence from Spanish colonial rule. Country spends most of the 19th century in violent power struggles between Liberal and Conservative factions.
1909 -- U.S. government supports a coup by Nicaragua's conservative forces, beginning a long period of U.S. occupations and interventions in Nicaragua.
1927 -- Nicaragua's national hero, Cesar Augusto Sandino, begins a rebellion against the U.S. occupiers and their Nicaraguan partners.

1934 -- Sandino forces the U.S. marines to withdraw from Nicaragua. Sandino is assassinated even though he had laid down his arms. Anastasio Somoza Garcia, at the head of the National Guard, installs a Somoza family dynasty. Somoza and his sons Luis and Anastasio Jr rule Nicaragua until 1979.
1972 -- Huge earthquake destroys most of central Managua.

1978 -- Somoza orders killing of Pedro Joaquin Chamorro, director of newspaper La Prensa, unleashing a wave of public protests. Sandinista National Liberation Front assumes control of anti-Somoza fight and launches general insurrection.

1979 -- Somoza flees the country, and a national reconstruction government is formed under Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega. Left-wing stance of Sandinista leaders results in formation of anti-Sandinista rebels, the Contras.

1984 -- Daniel Ortega is elected president in a vote boycotted by much of the opposition. The U.S. government led by President Ronald Reagan backs the Contra rebels with arms and money, escalating the armed conflict.

Inflation reaches 33,000 percent in 1988 and GDP plunges 13.6 percent. Central American presidents step in and broker a peace settlement. The U.S. disarms the contras in return for guarantees of a fair presidential election.

1990 -- Violeta Barrios de Chamorro at the head of an anti-Sandinista National Opposition Coalition (UNO) made up of 14 parties, defeats Daniel Ortega and is elected president. She installs a national reconciliation government. War ends and the economy gradually starts to recover.
